Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

=== key 2fa08f889fa2
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: It is unclear how much excluding alignment content from pretraining would change model behavior.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2023-09-05, on "Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/mLfPHv4QjmeQrsSva/paper-on-measuring-situational-awareness-in-llms?commentId=mhfkdMNohXDp3svFm PARENT (not his words): This paper seems pretty cool! I've for a while thought that alignment-related content should maybe be excluded from pretraining corpora, and held out as a separate optional dataset. This paper seems like more support for that, since describing general eval strategies and specific evals might allow models to 0-shot hack them. Other reasons for excluding alignment-related content: * "Anchoring" AI assistants on our preconceptions about alignment, reducing our ability to have the AI generate diverse new ideas and possibly conditioning it on our philosophical confusions and mistakes * Self-fulfilling prophecies around basilisks and other game-theoretic threats HIS COMMENT: Good points. As we note in the paper, this may conflict with the idea of automating alignment research in order to solve alignment. Aaron_Scher makes a related point.

I'd be keen to see more examples of the paraphrases, if you're able to share. To get a sense of the kind of data that lets the model generalize out of context. (E.g. if it'd be easy to take all 300 paraphrases of some statement (ideally where performance improved) and paste in a google doc and share. Or lmk if this is on github somewhere.) I'd also be interested in experiments to determine whether the benefit from paraphrases is mostly fueled by the raw diversity, or if it's because examples with certain specific features help a bunch, and those occasionally appear among the paraphrases. Curious if you have a prediction about that or if you already ran some experiments that shed some light on this. (I could have missed it even if it was in the paper.) HIS COMMENT: We didn't investigate the specific question of whether it's raw diversity or specific features. In the Grosse et al [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03296) on influence functions, they find that "high influence scores are relatively rare and they cover a large portion of the total influence".
